segments.text: The goal is the vortex3 password. The binary, /vortex/vortex2, is setuid vortex3, and all it does is exec tar with a fixed option bundle and up to three of our arguments — so tar runs as vortex3 and can read the password file.

The plan: make tar archive the password file itself. Tar does not follow symlinks by default, but we control two of its arguments, and one of them can be an option — dash h, dereference — which turns the following into a plain option.

I log in as vortex2 and check the pieces: id shows five thousand two, the password file vortex3 is readable only by vortex3, and /vortex/vortex2 is setuid vortex3 with the vortex2 group — we may execute it.

The file command confirms it: setuid ELF thirty two bit, not stripped. Running the binary bare, tar answers that it cowardly refuses to create an empty archive — so the wrapper really is tar, with our arguments appended after its own.

I disassemble main: it builds an argv array whose first three slots are fixed addresses in rodata — the tar path, an option bundle, and the archive name — then copies argv one, two and three of the wrapper into the next three slots, and calls execv. No shell, no environment tricks: the injection surface is exactly those three argument slots.

The rodata dump names them: slash bin slash tar, the bundle c f — old-style create plus file — and the archive path slash tmp slash ownership dot dollar dollar dot tar, a literal name with dollar signs that no shell ever expands. Only two of our arguments survive, because the third slot has to stay null to terminate the array.
The archive from an earlier run is right where the constant says: owner vortex3, group vortex2 — group writable, and group vortex2 is us.

I set up a scratch directory with a dummy file, then probe whether injected options survive: I pass use-compress-program with an id redirect as the first argument. Tar accepts it and runs it — but the output shows uid five thousand two only: modern tar drops the setuid euid before spawning helper programs. Option injection works; privilege through it does not.
So the privilege has to come from tar itself reading the file. I link the password file into the scratch directory.

First try: run the wrapper on the link and list the archive. The listing shows the entry stored as a symlink — tar archived the link, not the target, and a symlink as vortex2 in an archive read back by vortex2 reads nothing.

Second try: inject dash h — tar's dereference option — as the first argument, with the link second. Now the listing shows a regular file, minus r minus minus minus dash dash dash, owner vortex3, ten bytes: tar, running as vortex3, read the password file and stored its contents in the archive.

Extracting to stdout with the extract flag and capital O prints the file content straight out of the archive: the vortex3 password. The archive is group vortex2, so reading it back is ordinary work. Level two solved.
I log out of the gibson, and level two is done.
